courses.title: ARM Assembly & Microprocessors
courses.blurb: AUD-aligned ARM assembly from microprocessor fundamentals through registers, instructions, memory, stacks, functions, and exceptions.
courses.description: A source-grounded ARM assembly course aligned to the uploaded EECE340 lecture material, with guided practice, quizzes, and projects.

lessons.title: Microprocessors, architecture & performance
objectives: Define a microprocessor and distinguish architecture from microarchitecture
Explain why programs are converted to processor instructions
Relate IPC, clock rate, caches, pipelining, and memory hierarchy to performance
lessons.explanation: A microprocessor is a CPU on a single chip. The instruction set architecture (ISA) defines the instructions software can use, while microarchitecture describes how a processor implements that ISA. Performance depends on how quickly useful instructions complete, which is affected by clock rate, instructions per cycle, pipelines, caches, and the memory hierarchy.
examples:
; High-level code is translated into processor instructions
; load values -> arithmetic -> compare -> branch
commonMistakes: Treating architecture and microarchitecture as the same thing.
Assuming clock rate alone determines performance.

lessons.title: ARM RISC model, data sizes & register set
objectives: Explain ARM as a load/store RISC architecture
Identify byte, halfword, word, and doubleword sizes
Describe the roles of PC, SP, LR, CPSR, and banked registers
lessons.explanation: ARM follows a load/store RISC model: data-processing instructions operate on registers, while memory is accessed with load and store instructions. In the 32-bit ARM model, a halfword is 16 bits, a word is 32 bits, and a doubleword is 64 bits. R15 is the program counter, R13 is the stack pointer, R14 is the link register, and CPSR stores status and control information.
examples:
; R13 = SP (stack pointer)
; R14 = LR (link register)
; R15 = PC (program counter)
commonMistakes: Assuming data-processing instructions directly modify arbitrary memory locations.
Forgetting that processor mode changes which banked registers are visible.

lessons.title: Instruction syntax & data-processing basics
objectives: Read ARM destination/source operand order
Use move, arithmetic, and logical instructions
Distinguish register operands from immediate operands
lessons.explanation: Most ARM data-processing instructions place the destination first. Operands come from registers or immediate values. MOV copies a value, MVN moves its bitwise negation, arithmetic instructions perform calculations, and logical instructions operate bitwise. These instructions work on registers rather than directly on memory.
examples:
MOV r0, #5        ; r0 = 5
MOV r1, r0        ; r1 = r0
ADD r2, r0, r1    ; r2 = r0 + r1
SUB r3, r2, #1    ; r3 = r2 - 1
AND r4, r2, #0xF  ; keep low 4 bits
commonMistakes: Reading the destination as the last operand.
Using an immediate constant form that cannot be encoded directly.

lessons.title: Shifts, rotates & Operand2
objectives: Apply logical and arithmetic shifts
Use a shifted register as an ALU operand
Explain why shift-plus-ALU combinations are useful in ARM
lessons.explanation: ARM can shift or rotate a register as part of many data-processing instructions. Logical shifts fill with zeros, arithmetic right shift preserves the sign bit, and rotate moves bits around the word. Combining a shift with an ALU operation can perform scaling and arithmetic in one instruction.
examples:
LSL r1, r0, #2
LSR r2, r1, #1
ADD r3, r4, r5, LSL #2
commonMistakes: Using logical right shift when sign preservation is required.
Forgetting that a shifted second operand can affect flags when the S form is used.

lessons.title: Single-register memory access & addressing modes
objectives: Load and store words, bytes, and halfwords
Compute effective addresses from a base register and offset
Use base, pre-indexed, and post-indexed addressing for arrays
lessons.explanation: ARM accesses memory through load and store instructions. A base register holds an address, and an optional offset can select a nearby element. Pre-indexed addressing applies the offset before the access, while post-indexed addressing uses the current base address and updates the base afterward.
examples:
LDR r2, [r5]
STR r3, [r5]
LDR r1, [r2, #4]
LDR r1, [r2], #4
commonMistakes: Confusing the address stored in a register with the data stored at that address.
Forgetting how post-indexing changes the base register after the transfer.

lessons.title: Constants, pseudo-instructions & literal loading
objectives: Distinguish immediate syntax from literal-loading pseudo-instructions
Explain why some constants cannot be encoded in one MOV
Recognize when the assembler uses a literal pool
lessons.explanation: The # prefix denotes an immediate operand encoded in the instruction. The form LDR r0, =constant is a pseudo-instruction: the assembler may replace it with MOV/MVN when possible or load the value from a literal pool when the constant cannot be directly encoded.
commonMistakes: Assuming LDR r0, =value always performs a real memory load exactly as written.
Treating # and = as interchangeable syntax.

lessons.title: CPSR flags & comparisons
objectives: Interpret N, Z, C, and V flags
Use CMP, TST, and TEQ to set flags
Use the S suffix when a data-processing result should update CPSR flags
lessons.explanation: The CPSR condition flags record properties of results. N reflects a negative two's-complement result, Z indicates zero, C tracks carry/borrow-related unsigned behavior or shift-out bits, and V indicates signed overflow. Comparison and test instructions update flags without keeping a normal arithmetic result.
examples:
CMP r0, r1
TST r2, #0x1
TEQ r3, r4
ADDS r5, r5, #1
commonMistakes: Using C and V as if they mean the same thing.
Forgetting that an instruction without S may leave flags unchanged.

lessons.title: Conditional execution & branch instructions
objectives: Choose branch conditions from CPSR flags
Build if/else control flow in ARM assembly
Explain how conditional execution uses flag results
lessons.explanation: ARM condition codes use CPSR flags to decide whether an instruction or branch executes. A common pattern is to compare values with CMP and then branch using a condition such as EQ or NE. BL also records a return address in LR for subroutine calls.
examples:
CMP r0, #0
BEQ is_zero
B done
is_zero:
MOV r1, #1
done:
commonMistakes: Branching without first establishing the flags needed by the condition.
Confusing signed comparison conditions with unsigned conditions.

lessons.title: Loops & array translation
objectives: Translate simple for and while loops into compare/branch form
Scale array indexes by element size
Trace loop state through registers
lessons.explanation: A loop in assembly is built explicitly from initialization, a test, a conditional exit, a body, an update, and a branch back to the test. Array traversal also requires correct address scaling: word arrays advance by four bytes, while byte arrays advance by one byte.
examples:
MOV r0, #0
loop:
CMP r0, #10
BGE done
; body
ADD r0, r0, #1
B loop
done:
commonMistakes: Updating the loop variable after an unconditional exit path.
Using the wrong byte stride for the array element type.

lessons.title: Multiple-register transfers & stack organization
objectives: Use LDM and STM with register lists
Explain increment/decrement and before/after addressing modes
Relate PUSH/POP to a full descending stack
lessons.explanation: LDM and STM transfer multiple registers between memory and the processor. Addressing modes control whether the base address increments or decrements and whether adjustment happens before or after each transfer. PUSH and POP are stack-oriented forms that use SP; the common ARM stack is full descending, so it grows toward lower addresses.
commonMistakes: Assuming the written register-list order controls memory ordering.
Forgetting whether SP points to the last valid item or the next empty location for a chosen stack convention.

lessons.title: Subroutines, BL/BX & register preservation
objectives: Call and return from subroutines
Explain the purpose of LR
Preserve registers so caller state can resume correctly
lessons.explanation: BL performs a branch while saving the return address in LR. A subroutine normally returns by branching to LR, commonly with BX lr. Because a subroutine may need registers that the caller is using, required register values must be saved on entry and restored before returning.
examples:
main:
    BL process
    B done
process:
    PUSH {r4, lr}
    ; body
    POP {r4, lr}
    BX lr
done:
commonMistakes: Calling another function without preserving LR when the current function still needs its own return address.
Saving registers but restoring them in an inconsistent stack state.

lessons.title: Passing parameters & using the stack
objectives: Explain register-based and stack-based parameter passing
Trace stack layout across a function call
Separate parameter storage from saved-register storage
lessons.explanation: Functions can receive parameters in registers or through the stack. When the stack is used for both arguments and saving working registers, the function must keep the layout consistent so it can access the correct values and restore the caller's state. ARM procedure-calling conventions formalize which registers carry values and which must be preserved.
examples:
; caller places arguments in agreed locations
; callee saves required registers
; callee reads arguments, computes result, restores state, returns
commonMistakes: Changing SP before accounting for where stack-passed arguments moved relative to it.
Mixing caller-saved and callee-saved responsibilities.

lessons.title: ARM exceptions, interrupts & processor modes
objectives: List the ARM exception classes covered in the lectures
Distinguish hardware-generated and software-generated events
Explain why IRQ and FIQ have different priorities
lessons.explanation: Exceptions let the CPU respond to hardware or software events. The lecture set covers Reset, Undefined Instruction, SVC, Prefetch Abort, Data Abort, IRQ, and FIQ, with one vector-table slot reserved. IRQ is the normal lower-priority hardware interrupt and FIQ is the higher-priority fast interrupt.
examples: ; event -> exception entry -> handler -> exception return
commonMistakes: Treating every exception as an external hardware interrupt.
Ignoring the processor-mode change that occurs during exception handling.

lessons.title: Exception entry, vector table & return
objectives: Trace the automatic state changes on exception entry
Use the vector table to explain how a handler is selected
Explain how CPSR and PC are restored on return
lessons.explanation: On exception entry, the processor saves CPSR into the exception mode's SPSR, changes mode and control bits, saves a return address in the mode-specific LR, and transfers control through the appropriate vector. Returning restores the previous status and return PC. Higher-priority exceptions may interrupt lower-priority handling depending on interrupt masking and priority rules.
examples:
; CPSR -> SPSR_<mode>
; return address -> LR_<mode>
; PC -> exception vector
; ... handler ...
; restore status and PC
commonMistakes: Assuming the vector table contains the same kind of entries on every processor family.
Forgetting that exception return must restore both control/status state and the program counter.

courses.title: MATLAB Fundamentals
courses.blurb: MATLAB basics for engineering: arrays, matrices, scripts, functions, plotting, conditionals, loops, and switch/case.
courses.description: A course grounded in the uploaded MATLAB Introduction lecture, covering the command environment through core programming constructs and plotting.

lessons.title: MATLAB environment & command window
objectives: Explain what MATLAB is used for
Enter commands and expressions at the prompt
Create numeric sequences and evaluate built-in functions
lessons.explanation: MATLAB is a numerical-computing environment and programming language for manipulating, analyzing, and visualizing data. Commands can be entered at the prompt, and vectors can be generated compactly with colon notation.
commonMistakes: Typing display prompts into script files.
Forgetting that semicolons suppress command-window output.

lessons.title: Vectors & basic array construction
objectives: Create row and column vectors
Use start:step:end notation
Concatenate arrays and transpose a row vector
lessons.explanation: Row vectors use spaces or commas between elements, while column vectors use semicolons. The colon operator creates regular sequences, and the transpose operator can turn a row vector into a column vector.
commonMistakes: Using commas where semicolons are required for a column vector.
Choosing a step that does not move toward the requested end value.

lessons.title: Matrices & element-wise operations
objectives: Create matrices with rows separated by semicolons
Use matrix multiplication
Distinguish matrix operations from element-wise operations
lessons.explanation: MATLAB treats matrices as first-class values. Matrix multiplication uses *, while element-wise multiplication, division, and powers use .*, ./, and .^ so corresponding elements are processed independently.
commonMistakes: Using * when the intention is pairwise multiplication.
Forgetting the dot in ./ or .^ for element-by-element calculations.

lessons.title: Scripts & M-files
objectives: Explain the purpose of a script file
Create and run a .m script
Use scripts to organize repeated command sequences
lessons.explanation: A MATLAB script file contains a sequence of MATLAB commands. Scripts are useful when a calculation requires many commands or large arrays and you want to run the sequence again by calling the script file by name.
commonMistakes: Saving the script with an unexpected file name and then calling a different name.
Assuming script variables are automatically local like function variables.

lessons.title: Function files & local variables
objectives: Write MATLAB function syntax
Pass input values and return outputs
Explain why the function name and filename must match
lessons.explanation: Function files package a reusable set of commands. Variables inside a function are local to that function. The function declaration names outputs, the function name, and inputs; the function name should match the .m filename.
commonMistakes: Saving a function under a different filename than its function name.
Expecting local function variables to remain in the base workspace.

lessons.title: Plotting functions and data
objectives: Create an XY plot
Label axes and add a title
Plot multiple functions and use line styles and legends
lessons.explanation: MATLAB plotting uses x and y arrays of matching size. plot(x,y) draws the data; xlabel, ylabel, title, and legend make the graph readable. Multiple series can be plotted in one call, and line types or markers can distinguish them.
commonMistakes: Using x and y vectors with incompatible sizes.
Leaving plots unlabeled.

lessons.title: Relational, logical & conditional statements
objectives: Use relational and logical operators
Write if/end conditional blocks
Use else and elseif for multiple cases
lessons.explanation: MATLAB conditionals use relational expressions such as <, <=, ==, and ~=, plus logical operations such as ~, &, and |. An if block executes when its expression is true; else and elseif provide alternative paths.
commonMistakes: Using = when equality comparison requires ==.
Forgetting the final end for a conditional block.

lessons.title: For loops & indexed results
objectives: Write a for loop over a numeric sequence
Explain start, step, and end values
Store loop results by index
lessons.explanation: A MATLAB for loop iterates a loop variable over a vector such as m:s:n. If the step is omitted it defaults to one, and the step may be negative. Loop results can be stored in an array using the loop index.
commonMistakes: Using a step direction that can never reach the intended range.
Overwriting a scalar when an indexed result vector was intended.

lessons.title: While loops & termination conditions
objectives: Use while when the number of iterations is not known in advance
Initialize the loop variable before the loop
Update state so the loop can terminate
lessons.explanation: A while loop repeats as long as its logical expression remains true. The lecture stresses two requirements: the loop variable must already have a value before the loop starts, and the statements in the loop must change it so termination can occur.
commonMistakes: Failing to initialize the loop variable.
Forgetting to update the condition-driving value, causing an infinite loop.

lessons.title: Switch/case selection
objectives: Use switch for discrete alternatives
Add an otherwise fallback
Explain when switch can be clearer than a long if/elseif chain
lessons.explanation: A switch statement selects one branch based on a scalar or string input expression. Each case handles one value, and otherwise provides a fallback. The same logic can be written with if statements, but switch can be more readable for discrete named cases.
examples:
switch angle
    case 45
        disp('Northeast')
    case 225
        disp('Southwest')
    otherwise
        disp('Direction Unknown')
end
commonMistakes: Omitting otherwise when unexpected inputs should be handled.
Using switch when the decision is a range comparison better expressed with if/elseif.
